items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Identifies the wall’s position and main material, and its rigid nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cell wall as the outer covering of a plant cell and 1 mark for stating that it is rigid and made mainly of cellulose.

rubric.why: States important functions of the cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for shape or support and 1 mark for protection.

rubric.why: Recognises that substances can pass through the wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the wall is freely permeable or that substances pass through its pores.

modelAnswer: The cell wall is a non-living, rigid layer outside the cell membrane in plant cells.
It is made mainly of cellulose and has pores.
It gives the cell its shape and provides support.
It protects the cell and helps prevent it from bursting when water enters.
The cell wall is freely permeable, so water and dissolved substances can pass through it.

items.followUp: Explain how human activities can reduce biodiversity in forests.

rubric.why: Identifies forest clearing to make land for farming.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking forest clearance to agriculture or farmland.

rubric.why: Identifies cutting trees for fuel or wood products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning fuelwood, timber or logging.

rubric.why: Identifies increased demand for land and infrastructure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for population growth, urbanisation, settlements, roads or other development.

rubric.why: Gives another valid cause of forest loss.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any other valid cause, such as overgrazing, forest fires, mining or industrial development.

modelAnswer: Forests are cleared to create agricultural land and for human settlements.
Trees are cut for timber and fuelwood.
Population growth and urbanisation increase the demand for land, roads and buildings.
Overgrazing, forest fires, mining and industrial development can also destroy forests.

items.followUp: Explain how carbon dioxide and water are used during photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Locates chlorophyll and identifies it as the photosynthetic pigment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll is the green pigment present in chloroplasts.

rubric.why: Explains how chlorophyll uses light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs or traps light energy.

rubric.why: Explains the conversion and use of light energy in photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light supplies energy for photosynthesis and 1 mark for explaining that the energy is converted into chemical energy stored in food.

rubric.why: Makes clear that light is required for the process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that photosynthesis requires light or does not proceed without it.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in the chloroplasts of plant cells.
It absorbs or traps light energy from the Sun.
Light supplies the energy needed for photosynthesis.
The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy and stored in the food produced.
Therefore, light is essential for photosynthesis, and chlorophyll enables the plant to capture its energy.

items.followUp: Name two sources of iodine and describe its importance and the effect of its deficiency.

rubric.why: Gives suitable dietary sources of iron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming appropriate iron-rich foods, such as meat or liver and green vegetables or egg yolk.

rubric.why: States iron’s role and/or the main deficiency disorder.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking iron to haemoglobin and oxygen transport, or identifying anaemia as its deficiency effect.

rubric.why: Gives suitable dietary sources of calcium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming appropriate calcium sources, such as milk and other dairy products, fish or eggs.

rubric.why: States calcium’s importance and a deficiency effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking calcium to bones and teeth and identifying rickets or weak bones as a deficiency effect.

modelAnswer: Iron is obtained from foods such as meat, liver, egg yolk and green vegetables.
Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood; deficiency can cause anaemia and weakness.
Calcium is obtained from milk and other dairy foods, fish and eggs.
Calcium is needed for strong bones and teeth; its deficiency can cause rickets or weak bones.

items.followUp: Explain how the opening and closing of stomata help regulate water loss in plants.

rubric.why: Explains the change that draws water into guard cells and makes them turgid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that sugar formation or accumulation raises osmotic pressure, so water enters the guard cells.

rubric.why: Connects turgidity with stomatal opening.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that turgid guard cells curve apart and open the stomatal pore.

rubric.why: Explains the loss of water and resulting closure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that sugar changes to starch or osmotic pressure falls, water leaves, and guard cells become flaccid.

rubric.why: Requires a recognisable, correctly labelled stomatal diagram.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for drawing two guard cells around a stomatal pore and labelling the guard cells and pore.

rubric.why: Checks key structural details in the drawing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing the thicker inner walls facing the pore and thinner outer walls, or for including chloroplasts and clear labels.

modelAnswer: In light, starch in the guard cells is converted into soluble sugar, increasing their osmotic pressure.
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis, making them turgid; they bend apart and the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, soluble sugar changes back into starch and the osmotic pressure falls.
Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, making them flaccid; the pore closes.

Figure construction: draw a diagram 6 cm high and 4 cm wide, with two kidney-shaped guard cells facing each other around an open pore; show thicker inner walls beside the pore and thinner outer walls.
Add several small chloroplasts inside each guard cell; label guard cell, stomatal pore, thick inner wall and thin outer wall.

rubric.why: Defines morphology as the study of outward form or structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining morphology as the study of the external form or structure of organisms.

rubric.why: Defines anatomy as the study of internal structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining anatomy as the study of the internal structure of organisms.

modelAnswer: Morphology is the study of the external form and structure of organisms.
Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of organisms.

items.followUp: Define agriculture and name two branches of it.

rubric.why: Defines horticulture by the plants it involves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining horticulture as the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers or ornamental plants.

rubric.why: States horticulture’s relationship to agriculture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that horticulture is a branch or part of agriculture.

modelAnswer: Horticulture is the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants.
It is a branch of agriculture.

items.followUp: Why is a control group used in an experiment?

rubric.why: Identifies the control’s role as a basis for comparison.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the control provides a standard or basis for comparison with the experimental group.

rubric.why: Explains how the control helps isolate the effect being tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the tested factor is absent or unchanged in the control while other conditions are kept the same.

modelAnswer: A control is the standard setup in an experiment used for comparison with the experimental setup.
It does not receive the factor being tested, while other conditions are kept the same, so the effect of that factor can be identified.
